chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him):

Regarding two men who testified against a man that he stole, and his hand was cut off, then one of them returned and said, 'It was unclear to us,' both are fined the blood-money (diyah) of the hand from their wealth specifically. And he said, 'Regarding four men who testified against a man that they saw him having intercourse with a woman while they were watching, and he was stoned, then one of them returned,' he said, 'He is fined one-quarter of the blood-money if he says, 'It was unclear to me.' And if two return and say, 'It was unclear to us,' both are fined half the blood-money. And if they all return and say, 'It was unclear to us,' they are fined the full blood-money. If they say, 'We testified falsely,' they are all killed.'

key_terms.دِيَةَ الْيَدِ: Blood-money of the hand (compensation for amputation)
key_terms.شُبِّهَ عَلَيْنَا: It was unclear to us (claim of ambiguity in testimony)
key_terms.يُجَامِعُهَا: He had intercourse with her (context for stoning)

ai.seo_question: What is the financial penalty for witnesses who claim their testimony was unclear after a punishment is carried out?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the principle of 'shubha' (ambiguity) in witness testimony, distinguishing between partial uncertainty and perjury to determine proportional financial liability (gharamah) rather than capital punishment. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that mere doubt in witnessing does not equate to lying, thereby protecting witnesses from the full penalty of qatl unless they explicitly admit to falsehood. This ruling underscores the precision required in hudud cases, where the burden of proof and the status of witnesses are critically examined to ensure justice.
